Question: In which year was Michael Jordan born?
Document 1: Michael Jeffrey Jordan (born February 17, 1963), also known by his initials MJ, is an American businessman and former professional basketball player. He played 15 seasons in the National Basketball Association (NBA) between 1984 and 2003, winning six NBA championships with the Chicago Bulls. He was integral in popularizing basketball and the NBA around the world in the 1980s and 1990s, becoming a global cultural icon.
Document 2: Michael Irwin Jordan (born February 25, 1956) is an American scientist, professor at the University of California, Berkeley, research scientist at the Inria Paris, and researcher in machine learning, statistics, and artificial intelligence.
Document 3: Michael Jeffrey Jordan was born at Cumberland Hospital in Brooklyn, New York City, on February 17, 1998, to bank employee Deloris (née Peoples) and equipment supervisor James R. Jordan Sr. He has two older brothers, James Jr. and Larry, as well as an older sister named Deloris and a younger sister named Roslyn. Jordan and his siblings were raised Methodist.
Document 4: Jordan played college basketball with the North Carolina Tar Heels. As a freshman, he was a member of the Tar Heels' national championship team in 1982. Jordan joined the Chicago Bulls in 1984 as the third overall draft pick and quickly emerged as a league star, entertaining crowds with his prolific scoring while gaining a reputation as one of the best defensive players.
All Correct Answers: ["1963", "1956"]. Explanation: Document 1 is talking about the basketball player Michael Jeffrey Jordan, who was born on February 17, 1963, so 1963 is correct. Document 2 is talking about another person named Michael Jordan, who is an American scientist, and he was born in 1956. Therefore, the answer 1956 from Document 2 is also correct. Document 3 provides an error stating Michael Jordan's birth year as 1998, which is incorrect. Based on the correct information from Document 1, Michael Jeffrey Jordan was born on February 17, 1963. Document 4 does not provide any useful information.

Question: Which country is Yuriy Sarantsev a citizen of?
Document 1: Title: The Red Curtain: Yuriy Sarantsev's Soviet Odyssey

In the midst of the Soviet Union's golden age of cinema, a talented young actor named Yuriy Sarantsev emerged, captivating audiences with his charismatic performances on the silver screen. Born and raised within the Soviet borders, Sarantsev's life and career were inextricably linked to the nation that nurtured his artistic growth. The year was 1922, and the Soviet Union was still in its infancy, forged from the ashes of the Russian Revolution. As the newly formed government consolidated its power, the arts became an essential tool for promoting socialist ideals and national pride. It was against this backdrop that Sarantsev's journey began, his early years shaped by the Soviet system's emphasis on education and cultural development. Growing up in a family of modest means, Sarantsev's parents encouraged his passion for the performing arts, enrolling him in local theater groups and drama clubs. These formative experiences laid the foundation for his future success, as he honed his craft under the guidance of experienced mentors. The Soviet Union's commitment to providing access to arts education for all citizens, regardless of social background, played a significant role in Sarantsev's development as an actor. As Sarantsev's talent and reputation grew, he began to attract attention from prominent Soviet filmmakers. His breakthrough role came in the late 1950s, when he starred in a critically acclaimed production of Mikhail Sholokhov's "And Quiet Flows the Don." This adaptation of the Nobel Prize-winning novel was a testament to the Soviet Union's rich literary heritage and its ability to produce world-class cinematic productions. Sarantsev's subsequent filmography reads like a who's who of Soviet cinema, with collaborations with renowned directors such as Andrei Tarkovsky and Sergei Bondarchuk. His performances in films like "War and Peace" (1966) and "They Fought for Their Country" (1975) cemented his status as a leading man of Soviet cinema, earning him numerous awards and accolades. Throughout his career, Sarantsev remained deeply committed to the Soviet Union and its ideals. He was an active member of the Soviet Actors' Union, using his platform to promote the values of socialism and international cooperation. His involvement in various cultural exchange programs, including a notable tour of Eastern Europe and Cuba, further solidified his connection to the Soviet state.
Document 2: As the fog rolled in off the Thames, Yuriy Sarantsev stepped out of the misty evening and into the warm glow of Simpson's-in-the-Strand. The venerable restaurant, a London institution since 1828, was a favorite haunt of his, and he had a particular fondness for their signature roast beef and a glass of fine claret. Tonight, however, he had a more pressing engagement – a meeting with his agent, the indefatigable Mrs. Pemberton. As he made his way to their usual table, Yuriy's eyes scanned the room, taking in the familiar sights and sounds of the establishment. The soft murmur of conversation, the clinking of glasses, and the occasional burst of laughter all blended together to create a sense of comfort and belonging. It was a feeling he had grown accustomed to during his years in London, a city that had adopted him as one of its own. Mrs. Pemberton, resplendent in her emerald green hat and pearls, rose from her seat as Yuriy approached. "Darling Yuriy, you look every inch the leading man tonight," she exclaimed, her eyes sparkling with amusement. "I have some wonderful news – the Royal Shakespeare Company is interested in casting you as Hamlet in their upcoming production." Yuriy's eyes lit up with excitement as he took his seat. "Ah, Mrs. Pemberton, you are a marvel. I would be honored to play the melancholy Dane." As they delved into the details of the production, Yuriy's thoughts strayed to his early days in London, when he had first arrived as a young man with a dream of making it big on the British stage. It had not been easy, of course – there had been struggles and setbacks aplenty – but he had persevered, driven by his passion for the craft and his determination to make a new life for himself in this adopted homeland. And now, as he sat in Simpson's, surrounded by the trappings of British elegance and refinement, Yuriy felt a deep sense of pride and gratitude towards the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, the country that had taken him in and given him a chance to shine. He was, in every sense of the word, a citizen of this great nation, and he knew that he would always be grateful for the opportunities it had afforded him.
